blocks.title: What Your {{ AI Receptionist }} Agent Runs
blocks.description: One agent covers the whole lead lifecycle: first ring, quote, booking, reminder, follow-up.

cards.title: Missed Call Recovery
cards.description: A missed call triggers a text back before the caller reaches a competitor. The message carries the reason they called, the crew's next opening and a booking link that works on a phone.

cards.title: Service Request Intake
cards.description: Web forms, Yelp messages and after-hours voicemails land in one thread. The agent reads each one, asks the two questions your quote depends on, and drops the answers into the job record.

cards.title: Job Qualification
cards.description: Move-out or weekly? Pets, square footage, access instructions - the agent collects what your cleaners need before anyone drives across town. It also flags the jobs your crews should not take.

cards.title: Quote and Estimate
cards.description: Your rate card does the math. Per-square-foot pricing, add-ons and minimums come straight from your own numbers. The client hears a price on the first call, not after a callback.

cards.title: Booking and Dispatch
cards.description: Open slots come from Jobber or ZenMaid in real time. The agent books the visit, assigns the crew that covers that zip code, writes the job record, and holds the slot while the client confirms.

cards.title: Confirmations and Reminders
cards.description: Confirmation goes out on the channel the client used. Reminders follow 24 hours and 1 hour before the visit. Gate codes and parking notes arrive while the crew is on its way.

cards.title: After-Hours Triage
cards.description: Saturday 8pm inquiries still get answered. Urgent commercial calls route to your on-call phone; residential quotes wait for Monday with the visit already held and the address already confirmed.

cards.title: Quote Follow-Up
cards.description: Most quotes go quiet. The agent follows up on day 1, day 3 and day 7, then stops. Three touches, the quote attached each time, and the thread stays where the client can find it.

rows.leftDescription: Your crews are on-site and the office phone rings out. Voicemail collects a name at best, and the next cleaner in the search results answers on the first ring.
rows.rightDescription: The agent picks up on the first ring, on every channel. No hold music, no voicemail, no promise to call back.

rows.leftDescription: Cleaning quotes get compared side by side within the hour. Whoever answers first sets the price the others are measured against.
rows.rightDescription: Your agent answers the inquiry as it arrives, at 6am or on a Sunday, and asks the qualifying questions while the client is still reading.

rows.leftTitle: Quotes Go Cold in a Day
rows.leftDescription: A quote sent Tuesday morning is dead by Wednesday. Your office manager has 40 other things running and nobody chases it.
rows.rightDescription: The agent keeps the quote alive in the same thread, attaches it again on each touch, and stops once the client answers or says no.

rows.leftDescription: Calls, texts, web chat, Yelp and email each hold half a conversation. Context lives with whoever took the message.
rows.rightDescription: 98% of texts get read against 6% of emails (Sakari, 2025). The agent moves the client to SMS and keeps one history.

rows.leftDescription: Small operators lose $80,000 to $250,000 a year once lifetime value and referrals are counted (Allclean, 2025). Recurring plans get offered only when someone remembers.
rows.rightDescription: Every one-time client gets asked. The agent offers the plan that matches what it just cleaned, at your rate, before the crew has left the driveway.

items.question: How is this different from a cleaning answering service?
items.answer: An answering service takes a message and your office manager still calls back, qualifies the request and books it. The agent finishes the lead. It asks your qualifying questions, prices the visit from your own numbers, holds the slot in your booking software, and confirms it where the client wrote from.

items.question: What does the agent handle, and when does a human step in?
items.answer: The agent handles intake, qualification, quoting, booking, reminders and follow-up. It hands over when a client disputes a price, asks for a discount outside your rules, or reports damage. Those conversations route to your phone with the transcript attached, so nobody starts from the beginning.

items.question: Does it handle one-time cleans and recurring plans?
items.answer: Both. A one-time deep clean gets qualified, priced and booked in one conversation. Recurring work is the follow-on: you decide which service types get a plan offer, at which rate, and how long after the visit the agent makes it. Nothing is offered on service types you exclude.

items.question: Does it work for our cleaning type, including commercial walk-throughs?
items.answer: Residential, commercial, janitorial and vacation-rental turnover all follow the same shape: qualify, quote, book, remind, follow up. Only the variables change. Commercial inquiries that need a price after a site visit get the walk-through scheduled instead of quoted, with square footage and access hours captured first.

items.question: What does it do to our speed to lead?
items.answer: Replies go out in seconds on every channel, at any hour, including Saturday evenings. The practical change is that your quote reaches the client while they are still comparing cleaners, rather than the next morning when two competitors have already answered.

items.question: How long does deployment take?
items.answer: Between 5 and 15 days for most cleaning operators. Day 1 goes on the template and your numbers. The next few days are integrations and channel setup, tested against real inquiries. The rest is reading transcripts and tightening the questions your crews care about.

items.question: How do credits map to what we actually get?
items.answer: Credits are spent per resolved conversation and per minute of voice, so a slow February costs less than a busy May. Unused credits stay on the account. If most of your work is one property manager on a standing schedule, there is little inbound for the agent to answer - the payoff is in call volume.

items.question: Who owns the conversation data?
items.answer: You do. Transcripts, recordings and the records the agent writes belong to your account, and you can export or delete them. Retention windows are yours to set. Access is scoped per user, so a dispatcher sees the threads for their crews without the billing history.

items.question: Can the agent do more than lead handling later?
items.answer: Yes. The same canvas runs recruiting intake for cleaner hiring, client win-back campaigns and supply reorder workflows. Most operators start with lead handling and add a second agent once the first one is quiet. The conversational AI platform page covers how the layers fit together.
